title: Elevation and Baseball
text:
title: “Does elevation affect baseball hitting?” format: html —
The article Effects of altitude and atmospheric conditions on the flight of a baseball motivates this question. The plot below uses Lahman’s player batting data from 2010-2025 and stadium elevations to compare each hitter-season with the elevation of the ballpark in which it was played.

park_elevations <- tribble(
  ~teamID, ~elevation_feet,
  "ARI", 1086, "ATL", 1050, "BAL", 20, "BOS", 20,
  "CHN", 596, "CHA", 594, "CIN", 482, "CLE", 653,
  "COL", 5180, "DET", 600, "HOU", 50, "KCA", 910,
  "LAA", 160, "LAN", 267, "FLA", 7, "FLO", 7, "MIA", 7, "MIL", 593,
  "MIN", 840, "NYN", 12, "NYA", 55, "OAK", 25,
  "PHI", 40, "PIT", 743, "SDN", 13, "SFN", 13,
  "SEA", 30, "SLN", 450, "TBA", 42, "TEX", 600,
  "TOR", 250, "WAS", 25, "ATH", 25
)

Batting |>
  filter(yearID >= 2010) |>
  mutate(plate_appearances = AB + BB + coalesce(HBP, 0) + coalesce(SF, 0)) |>
  filter(plate_appearances >= 50) |>
  inner_join(park_elevations, by = "teamID") |>
  mutate(home_runs_per_100_pa = 100 * HR / plate_appearances) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = elevation_feet, y = home_runs_per_100_pa)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.18, size = 1, color = "#2c7fb8") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, se = FALSE, color = "#d95f02") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(
    title = "Home run rates rise with ballpark elevation",
    x = "Approximate stadium elevation (feet)",
    y = "Home runs per 100 plate appearances"
  )




Hitter-season home run rates by ballpark elevation, 2010-2025.

title: Why Baseballs Fly Farther at High Altitude
text:
2024 MLB Statcast fly balls and line drives (n = 62,145) grouped by stadium elevation.




Across all 62,145 tracked fly balls and line drives in the 2024 MLB regular season, baseballs hit at Denver’s Coors Field (5,180 feet above sea level) traveled an average of 290.1 feet—about 6.5 to 7.3 feet farther than balls hit in near-sea-level stadiums (283.6 feet) and mid-elevation ballparks (282.8 feet), with higher-elevation parks between 700 and 1,086 feet also sitting above sea level at 286.3 feet. As the second and third panels make clear, hitters at Coors Field did not generate this extra distance by swinging harder or lifting the ball higher: average exit velocity (92.5 mph) and average launch angle (27.3°) at Coors Field were virtually indistinguishable from lower-elevation stadiums across MLB.
Because aerodynamic drag increases with air speed, thin high-altitude air makes the biggest difference on hard-hit deep fly balls. Focusing specifically on solidly struck drives hit between 95 and 105 mph at launch angles between 20° and 35°, exit velocity (99.8 vs. 99.9 mph) and launch angle (26.9° vs. 26.9°) are identical, yet balls at Coors Field traveled an average of 384.1 feet compared to 367.2 feet across the other 29 MLB parks. That 16.9-foot boost in carry often turns routine warning-track flyouts into home runs or extra-base hits, explaining why Colorado built deeper outfield walls and still leads baseball in high-altitude offensive environment.
Several important limitations should be kept in mind when interpreting stadium-level averages. Elevation is not the only atmospheric factor affecting ball flight: game-time temperature, humidity, wind speed and direction, retractable roofs, and MLB’s standardized baseball humidors all influence air density and carry. In addition, Coors Field sits more than 4,000 feet higher than the second-highest MLB stadium (Chase Field at 1,086 feet), meaning MLB has a large elevation gap rather than stadiums evenly spaced across altitudes, and seasonal park averages still reflect small differences in team rosters and pitching matchups.

title: Stadium Elevation & Batted-Ball Flight
text:
How Does Elevation Shape Baseball Flight?
While our homepage shows that home run rates climb with ballpark altitude, MLB Statcast ball-tracking data lets us test why: do baseballs actually travel farther in higher-altitude stadiums, or are hitters simply hitting the ball harder? Below, we examine 62,145 tracked fly balls and line drives from the 2024 MLB regular season across all 30 ballparks, comparing stadium elevation against average batted-ball distance (bbdist), exit velocity (launch_speed), and launch angle (launch_angle).
Use the dropdown menu below to highlight an individual ballpark or compare several stadiums side by side in both the chart and the table. Hover over any point to inspect its exact Statcast averages.



Select MLB stadium(s) to compare (clear selection to show all 30):















Stadium Comparison Table








What Visitors Are Seeing
Average airborne batted-ball distance rises noticeably with stadium elevation—peaking at Coors Field (5,180 ft), with other higher-elevation ballparks like Chase Field (1,086 ft), Kauffman Stadium (910 ft), and Target Field (840 ft) also ranking near the top. Crucially, the comparison table shows that average exit velocity (~92–94 mph) and launch angle (~26.5°–29°) vary very little from park to park, pointing to thinner air and reduced aerodynamic drag—not harder swings—as a key driver of extra carry at altitude.
